name: Elara Dawnmantle
equipment: A broken longsword hilt wrapped in silk (her brother Aldren's sword)
A journal of her brother's sketches of the family estate
features: Divine Sense (as an action, detect the location of any celestial, fiend, or undead within 60 feet not behind total cover; also detect consecrated or desecrated ground; uses equal to 1 + CHA modifier = 4 per long rest)

Lay on Hands (pool of 25 hit points; as an action, touch a creature and restore any number of HP from the pool; alternatively, spend 5 HP from the pool to cure one disease or neutralize one poison; no effect on undead or constructs; pool restores on long rest)

Fighting Style: Protection (when a creature you can see attacks a target other than you within 5 feet, you can use your reaction to impose disadvantage on the attack roll; you must be wielding a shield)

Divine Smite (when you hit with a melee weapon attack, you can expend a spell slot to deal extra radiant damage — 2d8 for a 1st-level slot, 3d8 for 2nd-level, plus 1d8 against undead or fiends; maximum 5d8 additional damage)
Divine Health (you are immune to disease)
Extra Attack (you can attack twice, instead of once, whenever you take the Attack action on your turn)

Oath of the Ancients: Nature's Wrath (as an action, use Channel Divinity to cause spectral vines to spring up and restrain a creature within 10 feet; creature makes STR or DEX save vs spell DC 14 or is restrained; repeats save at end of each turn)
Oath of the Ancients: Turn the Faithless (as an action, use Channel Divinity to cause each fey or fiend within 30 feet to make a WIS save vs DC 14 or be turned for 1 minute or until it takes damage)
Channel Divinity (1 use per short or long rest — either Nature's Wrath or Turn the Faithless)
Spellcasting (Charisma-based, can prepare CHA modifier + half paladin level = 5 spells per long rest from paladin list; oath spells are always prepared)
Aura of Protection (you and friendly creatures within 10 feet gain a +3 bonus to all saving throws while you are conscious — this is your CHA modifier)
Position of Privilege (Noble feature — people of high birth treat you with respect; you can secure an audience with local nobles)

known: Speak with Animals (Oath of the Ancients)

personality.traits: I carry myself with the poise of nobility even when covered in mud and blood — my mother insisted that a Dawnmantle never slouches, and the habit stuck. I speak formally to strangers and warmly to friends, and the transition is so abrupt people sometimes think I have a twin. I unconsciously touch the broken sword hilt at my belt when I am making a difficult decision, as though asking my brother's ghost for counsel.
personality.ideals: The old alliances between the civilized races and the giants were not weaknesses — they were the foundation of a better world. Rebuilding those bonds is not naive, it is necessary. Justice is not vengeance; it is the patient work of building something worth defending.
personality.bonds: My brother Aldren died defending our estate from hill giants. I carry his broken sword as a reminder that strength alone is not enough — it must be guided by purpose. I swore my Oath of the Ancients after a vision of Annam All-Father weeping over his fractured children, and I believe I was chosen to help mend what is broken.
personality.flaws: I believe in redemption to a fault. I will offer mercy to enemies who do not deserve it, and I struggle to accept that some creatures are simply beyond saving. My noble upbringing also left me with blind spots — I sometimes assume others share my values and am genuinely confused when they act from pure self-interest.

appearance: Elara Dawnmantle is a striking woman of twenty-six with the bearing of someone born to command. She stands five feet ten inches tall, athletic and broad-shouldered from years of martial training, with the kind of straight-backed posture that makes her seem even taller. Her hair is a deep auburn, worn long but braided tightly against her skull in a warrior's knot that keeps it clear of her face during combat — a few loose strands always seem to escape, framing a face that is handsome rather than delicate. Her eyes are a warm amber-brown, sharp and perceptive, with the fine lines at their corners that come from squinting into bright sun across open fields. A thin scar runs along her left jaw from ear to chin — a souvenir from the night the hill giants came, when a piece of shattered masonry cut her as she dragged servants from the burning east wing. She wears well-maintained chain mail over a forest-green surcoat bearing the Dawnmantle crest: a golden sun rising over a mountaintop. The shield on her left arm bears the same device, though it has been scratched and dented by combat. Around her neck she wears a simple amulet — an eye wreathed in golden flame, the symbol of Annam All-Father, which she adopted after her vision. At her belt hangs her longsword, practical and unadorned, and beside it, wrapped in a length of blue silk, the broken hilt of her brother Aldren's blade. She never draws the broken sword; it is there only to remind her of what was lost and what she fights to protect.
backstory:
House Dawnmantle was not a great house. They held no vast territories, commanded no armies, and sat on no councils of state. What they had was a manor estate in the rolling foothills south of the Dessarin Valley, three generations of honest stewardship, and a reputation for treating their tenants well. Elara's father, Lord Marden Dawnmantle, governed his small domain with quiet competence. Her mother, Lady Cressida, ran the household with iron grace. And her elder brother Aldren — six years her senior, golden-haired and laughing — was everything a firstborn should be: brave, kind, and utterly certain that the world was fundamentally good.

Elara worshipped him. When Aldren practiced swordsmanship in the courtyard, Elara begged to join. When he rode out to settle disputes between tenant farmers, she rode beside him. When he spoke of the old stories — of the days when giants and small folk had lived in alliance, when storm giant kings had sat in council with human lords — she listened with wide eyes and believed every word.

The night the hill giants came, Aldren died proving that belief meant nothing without strength.

It was a raiding party — four hill giants, stupid and hungry, driven down from the hills by some disruption Elara did not yet understand. They hit the estate at dusk. The east wing was burning before anyone understood what was happening. Lord Marden rallied the household guard — twelve men with spears — and Aldren was first among them, his longsword bright in the firelight. Elara, twenty years old and trained but untested, grabbed a blade and followed.

The fight lasted eleven minutes. Elara knows because she counted every heartbeat afterward. Aldren killed one giant — drove his sword through its eye as it bent to crush a fleeing servant — and the blade snapped in the creature's skull. The next giant caught him with a backhand that shattered his ribcage. He was dead before he hit the ground. Lord Marden fell next, then nine of the twelve guards. Elara and the three survivors held a doorway until dawn, when the giants lost interest and lumbered away, bellies full of stolen livestock.

Elara buried her brother with his broken sword. She carried the hilt.

In the weeks that followed, as she rebuilt what she could of the estate, Elara had the vision. She was kneeling in the ruins of the chapel when the air turned thick with the smell of ozone, and she saw — not with her eyes but with something deeper — an enormous figure seated on a throne of clouds. Annam All-Father, the creator god of giants, father of all giant-kind. He was weeping. Not for the humans who had died, not for the estate that had burned, but for his children — all of them, every giant, scattered and confused and raging without purpose since the Ordning had broken. His tears fell as lightning, and where they struck the earth, flowers grew.

Elara understood, in that moment, that vengeance was not the answer. The giants were not evil — they were lost. The Ordning, the divine hierarchy that had given every giant purpose and place, had shattered, and without it they were chaos. The hill giants raided because they had nothing else. The great giants warred because they no longer knew their rank. And somewhere, at the heart of it all, something had gone terribly wrong.

She swore the Oath of the Ancients that night — not to a god of vengeance, but to the ancient bonds between peoples. She would find out why the Ordning broke. She would help restore it. And she would prove that Aldren's belief in alliance was not foolishness, but prophecy.
